title: Collapse Consecutive Identical Captures Into Expandable Date Ranges
body:
## Problem

Long-running profiles may produce many consecutive successful captures with no visual change. Showing every identical frame with equal weight makes the history harder to scan even though each capture occurrence remains important audit history.

This v0.2 issue is intentionally presentation-only. Physical artifact deduplication and storage ownership are tracked separately in #84.

## Desired Experience

- Group consecutive successful captures from the same project, page, and profile when their rendered screenshots are exactly identical.
- Show the group as a stacked capture card with:
  - a representative thumbnail;
  - an explicit No Visual Changes label;
  - the first and last capture dates;
  - the number of capture occurrences;
  - an Expand action revealing every timestamp in the range.
- Keep ordinary single-capture cards unchanged.
- Never collapse failed attempts into an identical-capture group.
- Never combine non-consecutive identical screenshots across an intervening change.
- Preserve access to each underlying capture record and timestamp.
- End an unchanged range when the next changed capture arrives.
- Apply the presentation consistently to the authenticated Compare workspace, built-in public galleries, and generated static galleries.
- Coordinate with #82 so the changed capture after a collapsed range receives the normal change-boundary emphasis.
- Coordinate with #83 so grouping behaves consistently across incrementally loaded history boundaries.

## Comparison and Navigation Behavior

- A collapsed group must expose valid Earlier and Later choices without presenting identical timestamps as different visual states.
- Expanding or collapsing a range must not discard the active comparison pair.
- Define how a deep link or restored selection reveals an occurrence inside a collapsed range.
- Pagination and incremental loading count underlying capture occurrences accurately while presenting grouped visual states.
- Profile and future page switching must never combine captures from different scopes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Exact consecutive identical successful captures render as one clearly labeled expandable range.
- The range displays accurate start date, end date, and occurrence count.
- Expansion exposes every underlying timestamp and capture record.
- Failed, changed, differently scoped, and non-consecutive identical captures are not merged.
- Comparison selection remains correct before and after expansion.
- A range that crosses an API page boundary groups correctly without duplicate or missing occurrences.
- Existing histories can be grouped without changing stored image ownership.
- Unit and API tests cover grouping boundaries, exact-match detection, scope, ordering, and pagination.
- Browser and renderer tests cover collapsed and expanded states on desktop and mobile across authenticated, built-in public, and generated static histories.

## Out of Scope

- Reusing, omitting, or deleting duplicate screenshot bytes; tracked in #84.
- Near-duplicate or threshold-based grouping that could hide meaningful changes.
- Changing GIF or WebM timing by removing repeated frames.

title: Split ranges in GRCh38
body:
I'm converting T2T-CHM13 coordinates to GRCh38 using CrossMap with [this chain file](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/human-pangenomics/T2T/CHM13/assemblies/chain/v1_nflo/chm13v2-grch38.chain) which I found [here](https://github.com/marbl/CHM13/blob/master/README.md).

My exact command is:
```bash
CrossMap bed chm13v2-grch38.chain.gz in.bed out.bed
```

I noticed that even though some of the input ranges are found in GRCh38, they are fragmented.

For example, the following range in CHM13
```
chr20	3,092,356	3,093,954
```

is converted to these 3 regions in GRCh38
```
chr20	3,061,544	3,062,830
chr20	3,062,833	3,063,134
chr20	3,063,134	3,063,144
```

The 3 regions in GRCh38 are almost exactly consecutive to each other, so how come aren't they merged into a single range? I cannot see any Ns in that region in GRCh38 (which could explain the breaking of the alignment used for generating the `chain` file, so I'm a bit confused...

title: feat: group contiguous signal bins into transmissions
body:
## Description

Implement grouping of contiguous detected spectrum bins into candidate RF transmissions.

Issue #2 produces a boolean detection mask indicating which spectrum bins contain power above the configured noise threshold. Individual detected bins are not yet useful transmission objects, however. Adjacent detected bins generally represent portions of the same candidate RF signal and should be grouped together.

This issue should identify contiguous `True` regions in the detection mask and convert each region into a structured `Transmission` object containing its frequency, power, and detection characteristics.

For example:

```text
Detected bins:

False False True True True False False True True False
            └───────┘             └────┘
          Transmission 1       Transmission 2
```

Each contiguous region should initially be treated as one candidate transmission.

This stage should describe detected regions but should not yet decide whether they are significant enough to keep. Filtering isolated bins, narrow detections, or other potentially spurious results will be handled in Issue #4.

## Requirements

- Add a structured `Transmission` representation to the `spectrace.detection` package.
- Group contiguous `True` values in a detection mask.
- Create one `Transmission` object for each contiguous detected region.
- Use the aligned frequency and power arrays from the M2 spectrum-processing pipeline.
- Record the number of detected FFT bins belonging to each transmission.
- Calculate relevant frequency and power characteristics for each candidate transmission.
- Return transmissions in ascending frequency order.
- Return an empty collection when no bins are detected.
- Validate that frequency, power, and detection arrays have matching lengths.
- Reject invalid or empty spectrum data with a Spectrace-specific detection error.
- Reject non-finite frequency or power values.
- Reject invalid noise-floor values.
- Require the detection mask to contain boolean values.
- Do not modify any input arrays.
- Keep the implementation independent of SDR hardware.

A possible API is:

```python
transmissions = group_signal_bins(
    frequencies,
    power_db,
    detected_bins,
    noise_floor_db=noise_floor_db,
)
```

## Transmission Representation

Introduce a dataclass representing a candidate RF transmission.

For example:

```python
@dataclass
class Transmission:
    """Candidate RF transmission detected within a spectrum."""

    start_frequency: float
    end_frequency: float
    center_frequency: float
    bandwidth: float
    peak_frequency: float
    peak_power_db: float
    noise_floor_db: float
    bin_count: int
```

This representation records the characteristics of the detected frequency region while preserving metadata that later detection stages will need.

It can be expanded in later milestones as Spectrace gains additional detection, fingerprinting, and classification capabilities.

### Start and End Frequency

`start_frequency` should correspond to the frequency of the first detected bin in the contiguous region.

`end_frequency` should correspond to the frequency of the last detected bin in the contiguous region.

For detected bins:

```text
Frequency:   100  110  120  130  140  150
Detected:      F    F    T    T    T    F
```

the candidate region spans detected bin centers from:

```text
start_frequency = 120
end_frequency   = 140
```

### Center Frequency

For this initial implementation, the candidate transmission center should be the midpoint of the detected region:

```text
center_frequency =
    (start_frequency + end_frequency) / 2
```

This represents the geometric center of the detected frequency region.

It is intentionally distinct from `peak_frequency`.

### Peak Frequency and Power

The strongest detected bin within the region should determine:

```text
peak_frequency
peak_power_db
```

For example:

```text
Frequency:    120    130    140
Power:       -40    -31    -37
```

should produce:

```text
peak_frequency = 130
peak_power_db  = -31
```

### Bin Count

`bin_count` should record the number of contiguous detected FFT bins belonging to the candidate transmission.

For example:

```text
Detected:

F F T T T F
    └─────┘
```

should produce:

```text
bin_count = 3
```

while:

```text
F F T F F
    │
```

should produce:

```text
bin_count = 1
```

Single-bin detections should still be preserved at this stage.

Recording the original bin count is important because Issue #4 will use this metadata when filtering potentially spurious detections.

The filtering stage should not need to reconstruct the original detection mask or infer the bin count from bandwidth.

### Bandwidth

Bandwidth should represent the frequency width covered by the detected FFT bins.

Because frequency-axis values represent FFT bin centers, bandwidth should account for the width of the bins rather than simply calculating:

```text
end_frequency - start_frequency
```

For uniformly spaced FFT bins:

```text
bin_width = frequencies[1] - frequencies[0]
```

and:

```text
bandwidth =
    (end_frequency - start_frequency) + bin_width
```

For example:

```text
Frequency bins: 120, 130, 140
Bin width:      10
```

represent a detected bandwidth of:

```text
(140 - 120) + 10 = 30
```

This also allows a single detected FFT bin to have a non-zero bandwidth equal to one bin width.

The implementation may validate that the supplied frequency axis is uniformly spaced before relying on this calculation.

## Example

Given:

```python
frequencies = np.array([
    100.0,
    110.0,
    120.0,
    130.0,
    140.0,
    150.0,
    160.0,
])

power_db = np.array([
    -51.0,
    -49.0,
    -40.0,
    -31.0,
    -37.0,
    -50.0,
    -35.0,
])

detected_bins = np.array([
    False,
    False,
    True,
    True,
    True,
    False,
    True,
])
```

Spectrace should identify two candidate transmissions:

```text
Transmission 1
  detected bins:     120, 130, 140
  bin count:          3
  start frequency:   120
  end frequency:     140
  center frequency:  130
  bandwidth:          30
  peak frequency:    130
  peak power:        -31 dB

Transmission 2
  detected bins:     160
  bin count:          1
  start frequency:   160
  end frequency:     160
  center frequency:  160
  bandwidth:          10
  peak frequency:    160
  peak power:        -35 dB
```

The second candidate is intentionally preserved even though it consists of only one bin.

Determining whether that single-bin candidate is meaningful or spurious belongs to the filtering stage in Issue #4.

## Testing

Add unit tests covering:

- One contiguous detected region.
- Multiple separated detected regions.
- A single detected bin.
- A detected region at the beginning of the spectrum.
- A detected region at the end of the spectrum.
- All bins detected.
- No bins detected.
- Correct bin-count calculation.
- Correct start and end frequencies.
- Correct center-frequency calculation.
- Correct bandwidth calculation.
- Correct peak-frequency selection.
- Correct peak-power selection.
- Preservation of the supplied noise-floor value.
- Transmissions returned in ascending frequency order.
- Mismatched frequency, power, and detection array lengths.
- Empty spectrum arrays.
- Non-NumPy input.
- Non-boolean detection masks.
- Frequency arrays containing non-finite values.
- Power arrays containing non-finite values.
- Invalid noise-floor values.
- Verification that input arrays are not modified.

Tests should use synthetic spectrum data and must not require SDR hardware.

## Architecture

This issue implements the third stage of the M3 detection pipeline:

```text
SpectrumResult
      │
      ▼
Noise-Floor Estimate
      │
      ▼
Threshold Detection
      │
      │ boolean mask
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Contiguous Bin Grouping │  ← this issue
└─────────────────────────┘
      │
      │ list[Transmission]
      ▼
Detection Filtering
```

For example:

```text
Frequency
──────────────────────────────────────────────►

Detection mask:

F  F  T  T  T  F  F  T  T  F
      └─────┘        └───┘
         │              │
         ▼              ▼
 Transmission 1   Transmission 2

   bin_count=3      bin_count=2
```

This converts the bin-level decisions from Issue #2 into structured candidate RF events that later Spectrace components can consume.

## Design Considerations

### Grouping and Filtering Are Separate Responsibilities

This function should group **every** contiguous detected region.

It should not reject a candidate simply because it:

- Contains only one bin
- Has narrow bandwidth
- Is only slightly above the threshold
- Appears likely to be noise

Those decisions belong to Issue #4.

Keeping grouping and filtering separate makes the detection pipeline easier to test, tune, and reason about.

### Preserve Detection Metadata

The `Transmission` object should preserve characteristics that are known when the candidate is created.

In particular, `bin_count` should be stored directly rather than reconstructed later from:

```text
bandwidth / bin_width
```

This ensures later stages operate on the actual result of the grouping process rather than attempting to infer it.

### Center Frequency Is Not Peak Frequency

The transmission's `center_frequency` describes the center of the detected frequency region.

The `peak_frequency` identifies the strongest FFT bin within that region.

These may be the same for symmetric signals, but they should remain separate properties because real RF signals may have asymmetric spectra or off-center peaks.

### Candidate Transmissions Are Not Devices

A `Transmission` object represents detected RF energy within a frequency region.

It does **not** imply:

- A device has been identified
- The signal is malicious
- The signal is unauthorized
- The signal belongs to a particular protocol
- The signal has been RF-fingerprinted

Those decisions belong to later Spectrace stages.

## Out of Scope

This issue does **not** include:

- Noise-floor estimation
- Threshold calculation
- Deciding which bins exceed the threshold
- Filtering isolated or spurious detections
- Minimum bandwidth filtering
- Minimum-bin filtering
- Minimum power-above-noise filtering
- RF fingerprint extraction
- Device classification
- Authorized/unauthorized device decisions
- Protocol identification or decoding
- Absolute or calibrated dBm measurements
- Continuous monitoring
- Persistent RF data storage
- Visualization

These responsibilities belong to other M3 issues or later milestones.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `Transmission` dataclass is implemented.
- [ ] `Transmission` includes `bin_count`.
- [ ] Contiguous detected bins are grouped into candidate transmissions.
- [ ] Separate detected regions produce separate transmission objects.
- [ ] Single-bin regions are preserved as candidate transmissions.
- [ ] Bin count accurately represents the number of detected bins in each region.
- [ ] Start and end frequencies are calculated correctly.
- [ ] Center frequency is calculated from the detected region.
- [ ] Bandwidth accounts for FFT bin width.
- [ ] Peak frequency and peak power are calculated correctly.
- [ ] Noise-floor information is preserved in each transmission.
- [ ] No detections produce an empty collection.
- [ ] Transmissions are returned in ascending frequency order.
- [ ] Mismatched or invalid inputs produce a clear detection error.
- [ ] Input arrays are not modified.
- [ ] Unit tests use synthetic data and require no SDR hardware.
- [ ] Full Spectrace test suite passes.

title: StatsAggregator: per-interval statistics are O(intervals x samples), slow for TimeWindowEvent with many windows
body:
## Summary

The query-engine `StatsAggregator` computes per-interval statistics with a full-length boolean mask per interval. Its cost is therefore **O(intervals × samples)** per channel and container. This was fine for events with a handful of instances per container, but `TimeWindowEvent` routinely produces thousands to hundreds of thousands of windows per container, so a scoped `StatsAggregator` can make the solve extremely slow or time out.

Found during code review of `feature/time_window_event` (TimeWindowEvent).

## Where

`src/impulse_query_engine/analyze/query/aggregations/stats_aggregator.py`

- `build()` calls `_calculate_aggregations(series, t_start, t_end)` once per non-degenerate interval and per input series.
- `_calculate_aggregations` starts with

  ```python
  mask = (sample_series.tends > t_start) & (sample_series.tstarts < t_end)
  ```

  which scans the **whole** series for every interval, and then indexes `sample_series.values[mask]` again for several statistics (`start`, `end`, `min`, `max`).
- `_calculate_cross_channel_statistics` clips every input series per interval via `series.where(Intervals([t_start], [t_end]))`, which is again a full pass per interval and series.

## Impact (example)

A 24 h container with 10 ms samples (8.6e6 rows) and 1 s windows (86,400 windows) means about 7e11 comparisons per channel inside one pandas UDF call. The default `max_windows_per_container` (1,000,000) allows even more.

## Proposed approach

The samples of a `SampleSeries` are sorted and non-overlapping (`tstart_i < tend_i <= tstart_{i+1}`). So each interval's samples form one contiguous range, found with two binary searches:

```python
lo = np.searchsorted(series.tends, t_start, side="right")   # first sample with tend > t_start
hi = np.searchsorted(series.tstarts, t_end, side="left")    # first sample with tstart >= t_end
```

Then:
- Compute all ranges at once (vectorized `searchsorted` over the arrays of interval starts and ends), and use slices (views) instead of masks. That makes it O(samples + intervals · log samples).
- Index `values` / `tstarts` / `tends` once per interval and reuse the slice for every statistic.
- Apply the same range lookup to the cross-channel path instead of `where(Intervals([...]))` per interval.
- Optionally vectorize the common statistics (`min` / `max` / duration-weighted `mean`) over all windows with `np.minimum.reduceat` / `np.add.reduceat` on the range boundaries.

Keep the existing semantics:
- the clipping by `SampleSeries.where(intervals)` upstream in `build()` (durations are already clipped to the intervals);
- NaN results for empty / all-NaN intervals;
- custom per-channel statistics still receive the interval's `SampleSeries` (possibly empty).

Check `SampleSeries.where` for the same per-interval pattern while at it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Results are identical to the current implementation. Add a property-style unit test that compares old (mask) and new (range) results on random sorted series and random interval sets, including empty intervals, all-NaN intervals, intervals touching sample boundaries, and overlapping intervals.
- All existing `StatsAggregator` / `TimeWindowEvent` tests pass unchanged.
- A benchmark (e.g. under `tests/.../benchmark`, or a documented script) shows the improvement for a large window count, such as 8.6e6 samples × 86,400 windows.

title: One-to-one mapping operator?
body:
Hello,

I want to track pedestrians using Rekall. So i am taking detections per-frame and comparing the iou of detections in the previous frame. I am using join to merge and update the intervals which has iou>iou_thresh. But join gives one-to-many mapping. Is there a way to make one-to-one assignments/mapping in Rekall?

Thanks
